title: John A. Strong
summary: John A. Strong is a historian and ethnohistorian whose scholarship has shaped modern interpretation of Native Long Island history, especially Shinnecock, Montaukett, Unkechaug, and broader Algonquian histories of land, labor, sovereignty, and survivance.
content:
John A. Strong (born 1937) is a historian and ethnohistorian whose scholarship has shaped modern interpretation of Native Long Island history, especially histories of Shinnecock, Montaukett, Unkechaug, land, labor, sovereignty, and survivance.

Source biographies identify Strong as a professor of History and American Studies at Southampton College of Long Island University, a Syracuse University Ph.D., and a Suffolk County Archaeological Association advisory board member.5 His research draws from town archives, deeds, petitions, court records, whaling records, archaeology, and Native community histories, making his work a major foundation for many place-based On This Site entries.6

Historical Work

Strong's books and articles challenged older myths that treated Long Island Native people as background to colonial settlement or as vanished communities.7 His work follows Native governance, family networks, land pressure, reservation history, whaling labor, legal struggles, and cultural continuity into the present.246

Major works relevant to this archive include The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island From Earliest Times to 1700, "We Are Still Here!" The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History, and America's Early Whalemen: Indian Shore Whalers on Long Island, 1650-1750.12346

Use in Native Long Island History

Strong's research is relevant to On This Site topics including Wyandanch and Montaukett diplomacy, Shinnecock land history, Unkechaug sovereignty and Poospatuck history, Native whaling, the myth of the thirteen tribes, and the survival of Native communities after dispossession.

Strong was a non-Native academic historian whose work is frequently cited in Native Long Island scholarship; he should not be treated as a Native community member or as the sole authority on the histories documented here.

why_this_matters: John A. Strong's work interprets Native Long Island through careful historical research rather than simplified myths of disappearance. His scholarship connects places, records, families, labor, law, and community survival, placing academic history in conversation with public memory and Native-led interpretation.
